lines.text: Chapter seven, section two. Scenario, defending with range advantage.
Picture the big blind defending against an under-the-gun open, and the flop coming eight-six-four with two clubs.
The under-the-gun raiser's range is heavy on high cards and premium pairs; it does not connect well with a low, connected board.
The big blind's defending range, meanwhile, is packed with hands that flop pairs, gutshots, straight draws, and combo draws.
That gives the big blind both a small equity advantage and a huge nut advantage: sets, straights, and two pair combos are all disproportionately in her range.
The equilibrium answer is not to check-call passively; it is to check-raise a real polarized range that punishes the aggressor's under-defended c-bet.
Pure value hands like sets and straight draws that flopped straights lead the raising range, with balancing semi-bluffs like combo draws and hands like nine-seven suited with a backdoor flush.
Meanwhile, the big blind should defend a wide calling range with pairs and mid-strength holdings that can continue on many turns.

The aggressor, seeing all this pressure, should respond by c-betting less often on such boards, but many real opponents still fire the standard c-bet, and that mistake is what the big blind is exploiting.
This scenario is a template: whenever your range dominates the board, become the aggressor even though you were the caller pre-flop.
